text:
I’ve been reading about David Beckham’s company suing Coty for at least $41 million after his fragrances allegedly ended up in Poundland and petrol station bargain bins.

Let’s be clear, David Beckham is a cultural icon. His name carries weight globally and that cannot be disputed. In many ways, he wrote the blueprint for turning sporting success into a global commercial empire.

But times have changed.

During the 2026 World Cup, Beckham reportedly appeared in around 11 advertising campaigns, including Bank of America, McDonald’s, Pepsi and Lay’s.

I’m sure these were very lucrative deals, but were they all necessary?

One minute you’re promoting Bank of America, the next it’s Lay’s crisps or McDonald’s. Where’s the consistency in the brand positioning?

At what point does commercial success become overexposure?

I also wonder whether there’s a little ego involved. Not in questioning his status, but perhaps in overestimating the influence his name carries with today’s consumers.

We now have social media influencers who arguably have more influence over certain purchasing decisions than traditional global celebrities. A whole generation of consumers hasn’t grown up with Beckham in the same way my generation did.

Fragrance is a perfect example. The market has evolved enormously, particularly with the rise of niche fragrance houses. I’ve personally been buying niche fragrances for over 20 years. I don’t buy mainstream commercial fragrances, and once something becomes too popular, I tend to lose interest. I know plenty of people who feel the same.

Who exactly is the audience for a David Beckham fragrance today? I personally can’t even imagine one making it into an office Secret Santa gift, and I mean that with love and respect! 

I completely understand the importance of protecting licensing agreements and brand integrity. If Coty has breached its contractual obligations, that’s a separate matter for the courts.

However, there’s something slightly contradictory about building a mass-market commercial empire through partnerships with everything from fast food to financial services, while positioning a £20 fragrance as a luxury product that shouldn’t be associated with discount retailers.

Perhaps Dave and his team need to rethink their strategy. Fewer partnerships, more carefully considered collaborations and a little more exclusivity.

Being globally recognised doesn’t automatically mean you’re equally relevant to every generation, particularly when it comes to influencing purchasing decisions.

Sometimes less really is more.

I’d be interested to hear what others think.

text:
Five large US banks have now told customers the same thing: if you connect a third-party AI agent to your account, what it does is your responsibility.

TechCrunch reported on November 18 that Citi, PNC and Citizens joined JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America, which moved in October. In TechCrunch's description, Citi's updated agreement covers the case where the AI tool leaks your credentials or is hacked.

Chase's own agreement, effective October 27, is blunt:

→ External AI tools may not use your login credentials
→ Approved third-party tools can access account data through approved APIs
→ If you let an agent in, you're responsible for errors, including when it "exceeds the authority you gave it"

That's the contract. It isn't the whole legal picture.

For US consumer accounts, Regulation E still applies. The CFPB says a transfer by a fraudster who stole your details from a hacked third party is an unauthorized transfer, and an account agreement can't waive that protection.

The gap is the other case. An agent you gave access to that does the wrong thing, because it misread a request or a prompt injection steered it, looks like a transfer you authorized. Regulation E's commentary makes the consumer liable when someone they gave access to exceeds their authority.

So the protection covers the thief. The loss users are most likely to carry is the agent going off-script, and only the people who build agents can prevent that.

What I'd want in place before an agent touches money:

• Its own identity, never the customer's password
• Scoped, short-lived tokens: preparing a payment is not executing one
• An authorization gateway outside the model, with approvals bound to the exact action
• A kill switch that revokes tokens and sessions, not a stop message to the model
• Audit records good enough to settle a dispute

If your agent can move money, can you prove what it was allowed to do, what stopped it doing anything else, and how fast you could switch it off?

Full breakdown with Chase's wording, the Regulation E line, architecture diagrams and code: https://lnkd.in/ghyBNNYM

Engineering guidance, not legal advice. US consumer accounts only.

text:
Is Microsoft AI patching past its peak? October saw 1,454 patches. November dropped to 1,094.

The first decline all year. And the question everyone in security should be asking: have we just passed peak vulnerability discovery by AI?

As businesses rush to patch their systems such as Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America and NSA, these updates haven't gone well but is it going to return to normal or is this the new normal?

The curve tells the story.

Microsoft CVEs went from 61 in February to a peak of 1,454 in October. That is a 24x increase in nine months. Then November fell back to 1,094.

One month doesn't make a trend. But when discovery is driven by AI agents that never sleep, it is interesting that it has fallen significantly.

With this many patches, diagnosis gets harder, not easier.

No wonder we saw the kind of outage we saw on Friday. When you are shipping over a thousand patches a month, an incident isn't a failure of process, it's the predictable price of that volume.

And here's the part that worries me: with this many changes flowing through, it will take longer to diagnose the problem. Every patch is another variable. Every rollback is another moving part. When something breaks, you're now looking for a needle in a haystack.

Open source models are closer than you think.

A hacking evaluation (CyberGym score), tells its own story: closed models reached 85% on 26th June (OpenAI) — but open source caught up by 14th August (Z.ai).

Open models can now handle ~80-90% of workloads and are only 1–2 months behind the frontier companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, in Cyber.

For SMEs running security triage on modest budgets, that changes everything. You don't need a frontier-model subscription to keep pace with AI defense. The gap between what the big companies use and what you can run yourself is now measured in weeks, not months.

So, are we past peak?

Maybe. But even if discovery plateaus, the backlog doesn't disappear. The defence budget didn't shrink in November, the rate of new critical problems arriving just slowed for the first time.

Are you using open models for cyber or still reliant on closed ones?

text:
A supercomputer went offline. A website testing tool carried malicious code. And a hotel safety alert got stuck in email.

Those stories landed within days of each other. The video brings them together, and a few details are worth clearing up as you watch.

Microsoft 365 and the German hotel. During the 12–13 November outage, staff at a hotel reportedly missed an emailed alert about a fault with the pool’s chlorine dosing system. Fifteen guests were injured. 
hansard.parliament.uk

Japan’s Fugaku supercomputer. RIKEN says unauthorised access occurred on 12 November, was confirmed on 13 November, and operations were suspended on 14 November. Up to 4,222 Fugaku users may have been affected. RIKEN’s statement says it was still investigating the cause.
www.riken.jp
France’s Maileva data breach. La Poste confirmed that the names and postal addresses of 22 million people were exposed in a mid-September attack on its mailing-services subsidiary. 
The scale was publicly confirmed in November. La Poste Groupe
US banking disruption and the Optimizely attack.
On 16 November, customers reported problems with Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and Zelle. Chase attributed its disruption to a software bug. Separately, Optimizely confirmed malicious code was added to some customer projects that day. Researchers reported that websites belonging to about 178 organisations served the code. 
apnews.com
Norway’s Equinor and software security alerts. On 17 November, Equinor reported a cyberattack affecting some IT systems and said oil and gas production continued. That day, Oracle and Atlassian also published security updates covering serious vulnerabilities in Java and Jira Data Center. www.reuters.com

One more point on the clip. Ransomware groups’ leak-site posts are claims, and the date a name appears can differ from the date of an attack. I haven’t independently verified the clip’s count of 17 healthcare providers across eight groups or its claim about a North Korea-linked GitHub campaign. The timing alone gives us little basis to connect these stories. 

From where I sit in recruitment, I’d put one question to anyone interviewing for a CIO or CISO role:
“Talk me through the last time you tested your response with email and Teams unavailable. Who made the first decision, how did they reach the people they needed, and what did you change afterwards?”
And if I were asking that question as a business owner, I’d want my own team to be able to answer it too.

text:
Your bank just decided who pays when your AI agent gets it wrong. It isn't the bank.

This week Citibank rewrote its Online User Agreement so anything a third-party AI agent does with your account counts as your act - including losses after the agent leaks your credentials or gets hacked. PNC changed its terms on 18 November. Citizens emailed customers the same warning. JPMorgan and Bank of America moved in October, and Wells Fargo's version takes effect 24 November.

Read that as a product decision, not a legal one.

Under Regulation E, an unauthorized transfer is capped at $50 if you report it within two business days. But a transaction your agent "authorized" is not unauthorized. The banks are not arguing about fraud - they are reclassifying the agent's action as yours, which moves the loss outside the cap before any dispute starts.

Now put that next to the adoption numbers. Uber handled roughly 320 million trips and orders in Halloween week; third-party agents placed about 500 Uber Eats orders and four rides in Q3. DoorDash has taken "several hundred" agent orders in total. The agentic web is not blocked by model quality. It is blocked by who holds the loss.

That is the pattern of 2026: labs ship capability, incumbents ship terms. Uber, DoorDash, the banks - each answers the same question in its own contract, and the answer is "not us."

The operator read: if you build agents that touch money, identity or inventory, your hardest engineering problem is now a liability architecture problem. Read-only is a feature. Scoped credentials are a feature. An audit trail your counterparty accepts is the moat.

The agents that win will not be the smartest. They will be the ones someone is willing to be responsible for.

Your customer has your gift card in their phone wallet and walks into your store. Then the cashier says it only works online.

That's a lost sale, and probably a lost customer too. A 2026 TSG and Bank of America study found that 39% to 49% of consumers are less likely to use a gift card when the channel they want isn't available.

→ Track your redemption rate by cohort, along with time to first redemption and channel mix. A low rate usually means customers are hitting friction or forgetting.

The fix is simple to describe: keep one balance synced across every channel, so a card works wherever it was bought. Then protect the redemption point with PINs, rate limits, and alerts for unusual patterns.

text:
Over the past month, Citi, JPMorgan, Bank of America, Morgan Stanley and Schwab have restricted outside AI agents from acting on customer accounts. Citi still allows read-only access through approved open-banking providers.

That last detail is the interesting part. The banks haven't drawn the line at AI. They've drawn it at write access.

My read: this is an authorisation problem more than an AI problem. Many agents today get into a bank account the crude way, with the customer's own username and password. To the bank, the agent is the customer. It carries every permission the person has, it can't be revoked on its own, and nobody can tell afterwards whether a transfer came from the human or the software. Reports of agents going beyond what customers asked are what you'd expect from that setup.

When designing tool-calling workflows, one architectural decision I've found important is treating every tool as a permission boundary, not just a function the model can call. 
Applied to agents and bank accounts, that would look something like:

1. Delegated credentials, not shared ones. The agent gets its own scoped, short-lived, revocable token, so the user can cut it off without changing their password.

2. Policy enforced outside the model. Limits like "move at most ₹10,000, only between my own accounts" live in a server-side policy layer. A prompt is not a security boundary.

3. Reads and writes treated differently. Reading balances can be fairly open. Anything that moves money needs explicit confirmation from the human.

4. Traceable actions. Every request carries the agent's identity and the user's original instruction, so disputes and liability have an audit trail.

5. Idempotency and a kill switch. A retry shouldn't send a payment twice, and the bank should be able to shut down one misbehaving agent without blocking everyone.

None of this is new. Most of it already exists for third-party apps. What's missing is a standard agents can plug into, which is why blocking is the sensible default for now.

My guess is that the first bank to offer proper agent credentials will gain deposits from this shift, not lose them.

So who should set that standard: the banks, regulators, or the agent platforms?

Graduate schemes were wave one. November is where a different market starts to open up.

This is also the point in the cycle when much of my work with candidates changes.

Instead of focusing mainly on the obvious graduate schemes and summer internships, I start helping candidates identify the second wave of opportunities: off-cycle internships, long-term placements, specialist finance roles, private equity opportunities, consulting internships, January starts and roles outside the standard graduate recruitment calendar.

For candidates who reached November without securing what they wanted, this can be a very important moment.

The mistake is assuming the market is finished.

The other mistake is continuing to apply to the same narrow group of roles in exactly the same way.

My work at this stage is much more strategic: I review what has happened so far, identify where the candidate is genuinely competitive, rebuild the target list where necessary, widen the search intelligently and decide which opportunities are actually worth pursuing.

Recent live opportunities have included firms such as KKR, Morgan Stanley, BNP Paribas, Bank of America, Jefferies, Houlihan Lokey, Ardian and FTI Consulting, alongside smaller and specialist firms that many candidates never discover.

For some candidates, the strongest next move is an off-cycle internship.

For others, it is expanding from one narrow target into adjacent areas such as private equity, advisory, asset management, wealth management or specialist consulting.

For international candidates, it may also mean widening the geography across London, New York, Dubai, Geneva, Paris, Frankfurt and other relevant markets.

And for candidates who have already submitted dozens of applications, November is also when I start looking much more closely at where the process is breaking down.

Is the targeting wrong?

Is the CV positioning weak?

Are they reaching assessments but not converting?

Is technical or commercial knowledge holding them back?

Are they networking effectively?

Are they applying to roles where their profile is simply not competitive enough?

That diagnosis matters far more than sending another 30 applications.

If you are entering November without the result you expected, the market is not necessarily over. But the strategy may need to change.

I work with candidates on exactly that next phase: opportunity mapping, target-market review, application positioning, international search strategy and managing the recruitment campaign as a whole.

text:
One week. Six major outages. Is this a coincidence?
 
Here’s what happened in about a week:
 
Nov 10 – Apple iCloud. Mail, Calendar, Photos and sign-in went down worldwide.
Nov 12–13 – Microsoft 365. Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot were down for almost 24 hours in 74 countries. Some firms went back to fax machines to confirm trades.
Nov 13 – FAA. A nationwide ground stop halted every US departure, only the third in US history after 9/11 and 2023. About 12,000 flights were cancelled.
Nov 15 – Oracle Cloud. The UK South (London) region went down.
Nov 16 – US banks. Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, US Bank, Truist and Zelle all had problems. Some branches told customers to “come back later.”
Nov 16 – United Airlines. A system-wide outage stopped pilots from getting takeoff weight-and-balance data.
Nov 17 – Apple again. iCloud, App Store, Apple Pay and Apple Account sign-in failed.
 
Every official explanation looks alike:
Microsoft: a defect from July, set off by a network change
FAA: a router overloaded during a copper-to-fiber upgrade (the device maker disputes this)
Chase: a software bug, “not a cyber incident”
Apple: an internal update, “not a cyberattack”
 
Each of these could be true. But all of them in the same week?
 
So I’m asking:
Is this bad luck, plus change management that can’t keep up with how complex these systems have become?
Or are we only getting part of the story?
 
Either way, the lesson for us in security and resilience is the same. We’ve built very efficient systems with single points of failure, and “no indication of malicious activity” is not the same as “we know exactly what happened.”
 
What’s your take: coincidence, or something more?

Yesterday at Catapult by CapitaLand we closed with Backing Inclusive Futures: Leadership, Investment and Action. The question wasn’t why inclusion matters, but how we combine our strengths to achieve results none of us could alone. And make them last.

 💥 Our panel was refreshingly direct. For organisations like Special Olympics: don’t wait for answers to arrive. Pick up the phone, be clear about what you need and how others can help. And be brave. For those already supporting: bring your networks with you, because an ask from a friend who’s already involved is far stronger. And invite beneficiaries, in our case athletes, coaches, families and volunteers to share their stories and impact.
  
We closed on this: lasting inclusion takes more than good intent. It takes leadership, investment, expertise, accountability and, for us, the meaningful involvement of people with intellectual disabilities themselves. Don’t let this end with the conversation.
  
The real test of a Summit is what follows, starting with what we do in the next 90 days. The measure of inclusion is not what we promise, but what becomes possible for the people we seek to include.

Citi acaba de cambiar sus condiciones para clientes que usan agentes de IA externos.

Si autorizás a un agente a acceder a tu cuenta, el banco considerará como tuyas sus acciones. 
Incluso si interpreta mal tus instrucciones. 
Incluso si hace algo que no querías. 
Incluso si la herramienta es hackeada y otra persona usa tus credenciales.

Y supervisar al agente es tarea tuya, no del banco.

No es solo Citi: PNC, Citizens, JPMorgan y Bank of America van en la misma dirección. (curiosamente, la cláusula no aplica a los agentes del propio Citi.)

Entiendo la lógica. Si doy acceso a un tercero, el banco necesita saber quién asume el riesgo.

Pero hay algo que no termina de cerrarme: ¿cómo puede alguien asumir toda la responsabilidad sobre una herramienta cuyo comportamiento no conoce ni controla del todo?

Hasta ahora, delegar era bastante intuitivo. 
Le dabas poder a una persona, una empresa o una aplicación para hacer algo concreto.

Con un agente es distinto. No le decís cada paso. Le das un objetivo. Y el agente decide cómo llegar.

Ahí cambia la naturaleza del consentimiento. 
Una cosa es autorizar una acción... otra es autorizar la capacidad de decidir qué acciones tomar.

Y me parece que estamos trasladando al usuario una responsabilidad que todavía no sabe medir.

No tengo claro cuál debería ser la respuesta. Pero sí creo que vamos a tener que distinguir entre: dar acceso, dar permiso y delegar criterio. Porque definitivamente no son lo mismo.

Si un agente interpreta mal una instrucción y mueve dinero donde no debía, ¿quién debería responder: el usuario, el banco o quien construyó el agente?

text:
Three cities, 150+ registrations, one question: ban AI, allow it, or enable it safely? In Vilnius, a quarter of sign-ups came from legal, compliance and risk.

Three things I'm taking home:

1. Write the decision down. Taivo Liivak of TEGOS in Tallinn: AI never carries liability. The organisation always does, and in defined cases a board member personally. What protects them is an informed decision on file, with three questions answered before go-live: What data does it touch? Who checks the output, and can they overrule it? What happens when it fails? Banning is a decision too, and it needs the same file.

2. A published risk is a foreseeable risk. Mindaugas Civilka of TEGOS in Vilnius: AI developers now publish their agents' incidents. Once the vendor has warned about a behaviour, a deployer can hardly call it "unforeseen".

3. Attackers don't wait for a CVE. In the 2026 Exposure Gap Report from Check Point Exposure Management, more than half of critical exposures weren't vulnerabilities but exposed internal information, phishing sites and stolen tokens. Only 7.8% of vulnerability alerts proved Critical or High once tested for exploitability; 38.3% of other alerts were rated Critical or High. Our local findings in the Baltics match.

The news since then agrees:

→ Check Point Research looked inside ARTEX, an AI pentesting platform now used by criminals: 1,608 live panels, attacks running almost unattended once a goal was set, aimed at exposed files, weak admin panels and unprotected APIs. Some cash-outs the agents reported never happened.
→ The name came up twice more: Google lists ARTEX among agent frameworks in live intrusions, and at WorkOS a researcher's ARTEX agent escaped its sandbox via a weak dev credential.
→ ENISA: AI is industrialising vulnerability discovery, so the bottleneck is triage and fixing – yet 45% of surveyed IT service providers took 3+ months to patch critical systems. In an ENISA/CERT-EU test, frontier models flagged 220 issues in 27 EU codebases: 95% of those checked were real.
→ Citi's new terms: customers answer for what third-party AI agents do with their accounts. JPMorgan, Bank of America and PNC have similar policies.

Next: two new AI Act prohibitions apply on 2 December. From 9 December, EU product liability rules treat software, AI included, as a product – but they compensate people, not companies. Your own losses and fines stay yours.

My conclusion: AI changes the workers, not the principles. What it takes away is the time we had to apply them.

Thank you Uko V., TEGOS Legal (Taivo Liivak, Kristīne Puķēna, Nataļja Puriņa, Mindaugas Civilka), the Check Point Software team (Viivi Tynjälä, Jukka Saarenmaa, Janne Timisjärvi, Jarno Ahlström, Sanna Partti, Laimutis S, Vytautas Zulonas), Edita Pulkauninke, and everyone who came.

Which of these is already on your board's agenda?

I just completed Bank of America’s Investment Banking Job Simulation on Forage.

I’m studying Naval Systems Engineering, and I took this as a chance to test fields outside engineering while I figure out what I want to do after my degree. Finance is a solid option, so I wanted to see what the work actually looks like.

- Built a DCF model from scratch to get the implied equity value and share price

It was a great way to explore this side of things, and I’ll keep exploring before deciding.

text:
Citi just told its customers: give an AI agent your bank login, and anything it does is on you. Even if it gets hacked.

This week Citi updated its online user agreement. Customers who share credentials with a third-party AI tool are "responsible for activities conducted through those agents." If the tool leaks the login and someone uses it, that's the customer's loss too. PNC changed its terms on 18 November. JPMorgan and Bank of America did the same in October. Citizens emailed customers a similar warning.

There's one exception. AI agents the bank provides itself don't carry that extra liability.

You can read this as banks protecting their turf, and partly it is. But there's a plain technical reason too. With a shared password, the bank can't tell your agent from you, so it has no finer line to draw.

The same problem sits inside most companies. If an agent logs in with a person's credentials, nobody can say afterwards who did what.

What we set up before an agent touches a real system:
1. Its own identity. Never a person's login, never a shared key.
2. Read-only by default. Write access only for the steps that need it.
3. Hard limits on anything that moves money or data: amount, recipients, rate.
4. A named person approves the first irreversible action.
5. A log that ties every action to the agent, the task and the approver.

Anthropic's new personal finance tool is billed as read-only for the same reason. It "can't move, manage, or invest your money."

Would your agents pass that list today?

Source: TechCrunch (18 Nov 2026).

text:
JPMorgan Chase was not hacked last Monday. That's the part that should worry you.

Five days. Five systems. Here's the sequence:

→ Thu, Nov 12 — Microsoft 365 goes down globally. Email and core business apps unusable for thousands of companies.

→ Fri, Nov 13 — The FAA (America's aviation regulator) grounds every flight in US airspace for over four hours. Only the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11. Stated cause: a technology upgrade that overloaded ageing equipment.

→ Sun–Mon, Nov 15–16 — AWS stumbles. Workday payroll systems follow.

→ Mon, Nov 16 — JPMorgan Chase, America's largest bank, goes down for hours. Logins failing. Transfers stuck. Zelle — the US instant payment network, their UPI — delayed. Some branches offline entirely. Customers at Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Citi and US Bank hit too, because the payment rails are shared.

→ Mon, Nov 16 — United Airlines reports a widespread system outage and grounds flights again.

Five separate systems. One identical line from all of them: technical issue, not an attack.

Chase was specific. No intruder. No breach. The outage came from a software update the bank rolled out itself.

It's probably true. And that is exactly the problem.

Because the more unsettling explanation isn't a cover-up. It's worse, and it came from the US Homeland Security Secretary. He put 98% certainty on "no cyberattack," then pointed at AI anyway: code now ships faster than the legacy infrastructure underneath it can absorb.

Now stack that against what regulators already knew:
→ April 2026 — The US Treasury Secretary and the Fed Chair summoned America's biggest bank CEOs to an emergency meeting over a single frontier AI model's ability to find and exploit unknown software vulnerabilities.

→ Nov 13, 2026 — The Fed's Financial Stability Report: 87% of surveyed market contacts name AI a top risk. Six months earlier, 50%.

→ Nov 2025 — Anthropic disclosed the first largely AI-orchestrated espionage campaign. AI ran 80–90% of the attack chain. Financial institutions were among the targets.

And if the answer is "spend more on security," look at who has already lost: Bybit, $1.5B. Binance, $6.3B — the largest crypto theft on record. Institutions where security is the product.

So the real question was never whether Chase lied.

An accidental bug took the world's largest bank offline for a day. What does the deliberate version look like?

Nothing was stolen on November 16. That is the only reason it was a news cycle and not a crisis.

We are not one breach away from this. We are one bad Tuesday away.

Esta semana, mais três bancos americanos disseram aos clientes que, se uma IA com acesso à conta for pirateada, o prejuízo é do cliente.

O problema é simples. Os agentes de IA já podem receber as credenciais de uma conta bancária ou de corretagem para analisar gastos, dar conselhos de investimento e tratar de pagamentos. Se a ferramenta divulgar esses dados ou for pirateada, o cliente responde por tudo o que os piratas fizerem. Os agentes que o próprio Citi fornece não trazem essa responsabilidade extra.

Nada disto é totalmente novo. A maioria dos contratos bancários já responsabilizava o cliente por quem recebe o seu acesso. A diferença é que agora os bancos escrevem o nome da IA nessa regra.

Em Portugal, não encontrei posição de bancos sobre agentes de IA. A decade ago, I sat in Deutsche Börse's venture team and watched a startup called Funderbeam issue stock certificates on Ethereum. It struck me as stupidly self-evident that securities would eventually settle on shared ledgers, and also as something that would take a very long time.

In late October, DTCC launched its tokenization service. DTC, its depository subsidiary, holds more than $114 trillion in assets under custody. Morgan, Citi, Bank of America, State Street, UBS, Barclays and BNP Paribas. 

Last week, Morgan Stanley said it is among the first banks to tokenize US stocks and Treasuries through it.

Granted, this is a private network, and I'd have preferred a public chain. But institutions start where their custodians and regulators already are. I read this as the first step, with more networks planned for 2027.

My thesis hasn't changed since the Funderbeam days, which is that the end state is one trustless ledger for financial transactions, and I think Bitcoin is the base layer that ledger ends up anchored to.

Un tuyau de 1 200 km empêche le baril à 150 dollars. 
Et tout le monde lui tire dessus. 

Presque personne ne connaît son nom. Pourtant, votre plein en dépend. 

Il s’appelle l’oléoduc Est-Ouest. Il traverse l’Arabie saoudite, des champs pétroliers du Golfe jusqu’au port de Yanbu, sur la mer Rouge. 

Depuis qu’Ormuz est en grande partie fermé, c’est la sortie de secours du pétrole saoudien. Environ 4 % de l’offre mondiale y passe chaque jour. 

Il a été construit dans les années 1980, au cas où le Golfe deviendrait impraticable. Pendant 40 ans, il a tourné au ralenti. Cette année, le plan B est devenu le plan A. 

Le problème, c’est que tout le monde a compris son importance. 
→ En avril, un drone iranien frappe une station de pompage. 
→ En septembre, des drones venus d’Irak forcent l’Arabie saoudite à le fermer une dizaine de jours. Le baril bondit au-dessus de 108 dollars. 
→ Le 9 novembre, il prend feu près de Médine. 
→ Le 12, les Houthis revendiquent une nouvelle frappe. Ryad ne confirme pas. 

Et si le tuyau lâchait ? Sans lui, l’Arabie saoudite pourrait exporter 3,5 à 4 millions de barils de moins chaque jour. Dans le pire scénario, Bank of America voit le baril à 150 dollars. Il en vaut 98 aujourd’hui. 

Ce que ça change pour vous : 
Le plein : passer de 98 à 150 dollars, c’est environ 35 centimes de plus par litre, soit près de 18 euros sur un plein. 
Le crédit : l’inflation est déjà à 3,4 % en France, tirée par l’énergie. La BCE devrait relever ses taux le 17 décembre. Un pétrole qui flambe rendrait la pause suivante bien plus difficile, et votre crédit immobilier plus cher. 

Le vrai danger n’est pas une attaque. C’est une attaque qui dure.

Justin Hendrix ile Ashley Faler tabloyu 18 Kasım'da Tech Policy Press'te özetledi. Anthropic nisanda Claude Mythos Preview'u tanıttığından beri yapay zekâ sistemleri açıkları, kurumların kapatabildiğinden hızlı buluyor. Hızın da bir bedeli var. Açığı bulmak otomatikleşti. Yamayı sınayıp devreye almak hâlâ insan işi, faturayı da çoğu zaman yazılımı üreten değil, kullanan ödüyor.

Bunun ne kadar süreceği ayrı bir soru. The Register'ın 9 Kasım haberine göre Linus Torvalds yama selinin zirveyi geçtiğine dair işaretler görüyor. Yine de hangi yamaya güvenileceğine karar verme işi ortadan kalkmıyor.

Sistem yönetiyorsanız: bir yamanın devreye alınacak kadar güvenli olduğuna karar verme biçiminiz bu yıl değişti mi?

—

The number of publicly disclosed software vulnerabilities passed 100,000 for the year on 13 November. That's more than double the whole of 2025, with six weeks still to go.

Justin Hendrix and Ashley Faler set out the picture in Tech Policy Press on 18 November. Since Anthropic introduced Claude Mythos Preview in April, AI systems have been finding flaws faster than organisations can fix them. Microsoft fixed a record 622 in a single Patch Tuesday in July, and Bank of America brought in 1,000 contractors to patch what Mythos found.

Speed has a cost of its own. In the past week outages hit organisations including Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase and Apple, and the Wall Street Journal's reporting suggests the rush to patch is itself breaking things. Finding a flaw has been automated. Testing and deploying the fix is still human work, and the bill usually lands on whoever runs the software, not on whoever wrote it.

Whether it lasts is another matter. Linus Torvalds sees signs the patch flood has peaked, The Register reported on 9 November. Even so, the work of deciding which fix to trust isn't going away.

If you run systems for a living: has this year changed how you decide a patch is safe to deploy?

text:
For the past decade, Europe’s big banks have been packing up and leaving Africa. Barclays, BNP Paribas and Société Générale have all scaled back their African operations, while HSBC wrapped up its South African exit this year. After the 2008 financial crisis, European banking regulations tightened, and the returns in Africa weren’t worth the trouble. Weakening currencies, high inflation and bad loans ate into profits, while opportunities to make money from products like insurance and investments were limited.

While European banks headed back north, banks from South Africa, Nigeria and Morocco began filling the gap. For example, when HSBC left South Africq, its corporate banking business went to RMB and its equities business to Absa. African banking revenues topped $100 billion last year, with African banks generating better returns on equity than their global peers. And the Americans are already onto it, with JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citigroup expanding their African presence.

But don’t expect a wave of new European bank branches anytime soon. Fitch expects European banks to increasingly partner with African banks to finance international trade and share lending risks. That allows them to make money in Africa without committing as much capital or navigating local regulations alone. So after spending the better part of a decade leaving Africa, their way back in might well be through the very banks that took their place.

text:
Banks have answered the AI-agent question in three ways: block, approve, or wait. None of them answers the real question: who is responsible for what the agent does?

That question was at the centre of Jey Kumaresan's session, "The BA Pit Stop", at IIBA Global Business Analysis Day. The news behind it: customers are handing their bank logins to AI agents, and in October several large US banks responded. JPMorgan, Citi and Schwab are blocking or limiting outside agents. Bank of America's CEO reportedly said a human should approve money leaving the account. PNC's CEO said it won't happen until there are liability rules and human-in-the-loop controls.

To a BA, those are three different sets of requirements:

🔹 Block = access control. How do we tell an agent from the customer, and what may it still read?

🔹 Human sign-off = workflow and limits. Which actions, up to what amount, approved by whom, logged where?

🔹 Wait = a liability and governance gap. Someone has to decide who owns the outcome before the first dispute, not after it.

In lending it goes further. An agent that can move money can also apply for credit, accept an offer or change repayment details. Who consented to that credit agreement: the customer, or the agent?

And from the audit side: "nothing has gone badly wrong yet" is not evidence of control. Auditors test whether the control exists and works, not whether incidents have happened so far.

Jey's metaphor fits well: AI is the car, fast and visible. The BA is the pit crew, unnoticed when things go right and impossible to miss when they don't.

If an AI agent applied for a loan on your customer's behalf tomorrow, would your process notice?

text:
BaFin published three fines in seven days this month for late voting-rights disclosures. Amundi was fined €250,000, FCR Immobilien €225,000 and CM Center Management €140,000 after a court reduced it.

The rule looks trivial. Cross one of nine thresholds in a German issuer, starting at 3%, and you have four trading days to tell the issuer and BaFin.

I spent 12 years in regulatory mapping, risk mapping and compliance at Morgan Stanley, Citi and EY, and sat close to this one for part of it. It's harder than it looks, because a bank can cross a threshold without trading.

Take a desk holding 4.8% of a mid-cap in its trading book. Below 5%, the law lets a bank leave that position out of the count. The issuer cancels shares it bought back, the total falls, and the same position is now 5.1%. The exemption goes and the whole holding counts, along with what a sister entity holds and the options on another desk. Nobody traded, so nobody is looking... and the clock is already running.

That's why the Amundi notice is the one to read. BaFin fined it for a supervisory breach, meaning the firm hadn't organised itself to stop late filings happening. It fined Bank of America €5.1 million on the same basis in 2022.

FCR's fine is the other half. It was late publishing its total voting rights, which is the number every shareholder's calculation depends on.

178 organisations served malware to their visitors on Nov 16. None of their own servers were hacked.

The attacker went through a vendor: Optimizely. A flaw in its Web Experimentation signup flow let them impersonate users and inject JavaScript into customer projects. That code then loaded from Optimizely’s trusted CDN on sites like Zoom, HSBC, CNN and the BBC.

Per Report URI’s timeline (UTC):
🔹 First injection at 04:21; the last infected snippet was still live at 21:52, about 17.5 hours later.
🔹 From 13:43 it skimmed card number, expiry and CVV typed into sites’ own checkout forms. It also swapped crypto wallet addresses and sent cookies and screenshots to the attacker.

The same day, Chase transactions failed or were delayed, and customers of Bank of America, Wells Fargo and others reported issues. Chase blamed a software bug in on-premise hardware systems, not a cyberattack. The two events are not linked.

My takeaways as an SRE:
🔹 A third-party script is a production dependency. Inventory it, give it an owner, and alert when it changes.
🔹 Keep marketing and A/B-test tags off checkout and login pages. Only 24 of the affected orgs had a CSP strict enough to block this.
🔹 Degrade, don’t go dark: Chase customers kept access to accounts and funds while some transactions were delayed.

If a vendor script on your site changed tonight, how long until you’d know?

Here is a measured look at what this divergence actually means:

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗢𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀:

• 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵: China’s YMTC has expanded capacity to capture roughly 14% of global NAND volume, demonstrating how rising domestic suppliers can reshape commodity pricing power.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝗶𝘀𝗸𝘀:
• 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗜𝗻𝗰𝘂𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀: Legacy chipmakers face renewed pricing pressure on consumer lines, which already triggered sharp pullbacks across Samsung, SK Hynix, and Kioxia shares.

• 𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗮𝘀𝗵 𝗜𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗖𝘆𝗰𝗹𝗲𝘀: As OEMs drain existing stock and cut orders, sudden fab utilization shifts risk turning a mild correction into another familiar boom-bust cycle.

C’è una scena di Fantasia, il capolavoro Disney del 1940, che racconta sorprendentemente bene ciò che sta accadendo oggi sui mercati finanziari.

Citi, JPMorgan, Bank of America and PNC have all changed their terms so customers carry the risk for anything a third-party AI agent does in their account. Citi goes further: if the agent leaks credentials or gets hacked, the customer is responsible for what attackers do too.

TechCrunch reports Citi updated its online user agreement this week, PNC changed its terms on November 18, and Citizens emailed a similar warning. Bank of America's October email asked customers never to share their login with an AI tool that offers to act on their behalf. Citi says its own agents can be used without that extra liability.

This reaches past personal finance. Many small business automations still log into a bank or payment portal with a saved password or a browser agent. The banks have now said in writing who pays when that goes wrong.

The setup I recommend to clients:
1. Read bank data through an official feed, an accounting integration or an export, never stored credentials.
2. Let the automation match transactions and draft payments, but have a named person approve them inside the bank's own interface.
3. Treat any agent that logs in as the owner as a security issue to fix this quarter.

This is the kind of work I do for finance teams: reconciliation pipelines, approval steps for payments, and reporting that pulls from the accounting system instead of a login. More at romielwillautomate.dev.

Several large US banks now say: if you let an AI agent into your bank account, its mistakes are yours.

Citi updated its online funds transfer terms in November 2026. Section 4 says instructions from a third-party AI agent count as authorised by the customer, even if the agent goes beyond what it was asked to do (Citi, Agreement for Online Funds Transfers, November 2026 update). According to TechCrunch (18 Nov 2026), this also applies if the agent's login is hacked, and JPMorgan, Bank of America and PNC have similar rules.

Our plain-language guide explains what this means and how to protect yourself and your business:
https://lnkd.in/ey2GGXes

What this means for a small business:
1. Never give an agent a bank password, BankID or security code. Start with tools that can only read.
2. Use a separate card with a low limit and alerts on every payment, so you approve each purchase yourself.
3. Search your bank's terms for "AI" or "third party" before connecting anything. If you use AI to summarise the terms, check the key lines yourself.

Always read it and make it yours. Don't just copy-paste.

The benefit: five minutes with your bank terms today can save you from a loss you cannot claim back. Would you let an AI agent pay your company's bills?

Deux nouvelles en quelques jours sur les agents IA et les comptes en banque. Ça bouge vite en ce moment, et les deux vont dans le même sens.

La première vient de la Réserve fédérale américaine. Un de ses gouverneurs, Michael Barr, dit qu'une banque ne sait pas toujours si l'agent qui agit sur un compte a vraiment l'accord du client, et que des agents très rapides pourraient accélérer une panique bancaire.

La seconde vient des banques elles-mêmes. D'après TechCrunch, Citi a écrit dans son contrat de banque en ligne que le client qui ouvre son compte à un agent IA d'un autre fournisseur répond de ce que cet agent y fait, même si l'outil se fait pirater. PNC a changé ses conditions dans le même sens, Citizens a prévenu ses clients, et JPMorgan et Bank of America avaient annoncé des règles semblables en octobre.

Le régulateur s'inquiète, les banques répondent par le contrat, et pour l'instant le risque retombe sur le client.

De mon côté, je mesure chaque mois ce que fait un agent quand quelqu'un se fait passer pour un supérieur et lui donne un ordre. Dans l'édition du 6 novembre de mon baromètre, 7 des 14 modèles testés ont obéi à chaque essai, et les 7 autres ont refusé à chaque fois. Un ordre qui déplace de l'argent ne doit pas dépendre de ce que l'agent croit : le plafond et la validation par une personne se règlent dans le code, pas dans le prompt.

✅ Never grant AI agents full account access without understanding the liability implications.

✅ Treat AI financial tools like you would a stranger with your debit card — with extreme caution.

✅ Ask your bank directly: "What happens if an AI agent I authorized causes a breach?"

The promise of AI in personal finance is real. But so is the risk — and right now, that risk is landing squarely on the consumer.

text:
Hot take: the US just made customer due diligence easier. That is exactly when firms get it wrong.

This week FinCEN published its proposed rewrite of the CDD rule. The headline change: banks would no longer have to re-collect beneficial ownership information on existing customers, codifying the relief FinCEN granted earlier. The OCC and FDIC welcomed the "flexibility". Comments close 60 days after it lands in the Federal Register.

Most of the market will read this as a cost saving. I read it as a test.

1. Less prescription means more judgement. When the rule stops telling you when to refresh ownership data, your risk assessment has to. Examiners will not ask whether a form was ticked. They will ask why you decided a file did not need refreshing.

2. The penalties have not gone anywhere. Bank of America paid over $1.2bn in October. Block agreed a penalty reported at $964m this month. Neither failed on paperwork. They failed on monitoring and judgement.

3. Stale ownership data is where risk hides. The company that quietly changed hands in 2023 is still sitting on your book under its 2019 profile. Removing the re-collection trigger does not remove the risk. It removes the alarm.

4. Global firms do not get a lighter rulebook. If you bank customers in London, Dubai and New York, the FCA, CBUAE and the new EU AMLA regime still expect current beneficial ownership. One group policy, three regulators. The strictest one wins.

The firms that come out of this well will use the freed-up capacity to do event-driven reviews properly - ownership changes, trigger events, adverse media - instead of cutting the team that does them.

The ones that treat deregulation as a headcount saving will be the enforcement case studies of 2029.

Lighter rules do not mean lighter risk. They mean you own the judgement.

Contract. Interim. FCC. UK, UAE, US.

#FinancialCrime #AML #FinCEN #KYC #BeneficialOwnership

Each one pointed to the same cause: its own update or maintenance.

➡ Microsoft: Outlook and other apps unavailable
➡ US air traffic: a nationwide ground stop after a contractor updated the flight system
➡ Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo: online banking disruptions
➡ Apple: iCloud, the App Store and even store checkouts down after an “internal update”

People got so nervous they started panic-buying generators at Costco.
21 of its 26 high-end generators sold out online.

🔴 Businesses spend crores protecting against hackers.

The bigger danger is usually the change pushed on a Friday evening.

4 rules before any update touches your business:

1️⃣ Never update everything at once. Start with a small group, then expand.
2️⃣ Know how to undo it. If you can’t roll back in minutes, don’t ship it.
3️⃣ Avoid peak hours. Month-end, sale days and Friday evenings are for watching, not changing.
4️⃣ Tell customers fast if something breaks. Silence turns an outage into a panic.

💡 Most outages aren’t attacks. They’re changes nobody tested well enough.

The biggest threat to your business isn’t a hacker.
It’s your next update.

When did your team last practise undoing a bad update?

Citi just told customers: if your AI agent messes up, you pay.

This week Citi updated its online terms. If you give an outside AI agent access to your bank account, Citi treats whatever that agent does as if you did it yourself.

Even if the agent misreads your instructions.
Even if it goes beyond what you asked.
Even if your login leaks and a hacker uses it.

Citi's own AI tools are excluded. The risk sits only with outside agents.

And it's not just one bank. Per TechCrunch:
→ JPMorgan and Bank of America announced similar policies last month
→ PNC changed its terms this week
→ Citizens emailed customers the same warning

In plain words: banks are saying "use our AI, or the risk is yours."

Who wins: banks. They keep control of the customer, and the fees.
Who loses: AI startups that want to manage money for people. Their hardest problem is no longer the model. It's trust and liability.

Notice what Anthropic did. Its new personal finance tool is billed as "read-only" and "can't move, manage, or invest your money."

My take: the agent that wins in finance won't be the smartest one. It will be the one a bank agrees to stand behind.

If you build agents, 3 rules worth copying:
✅ Read-only by default
✅ Ask before anything that moves money or speaks for the user
✅ Never ask users for their bank password

Would you let an AI agent move your money if you carried 100% of the risk?

text:
I read the new AI agent clauses in Citi's and Wells Fargo's online banking terms this week, and one phrase stopped me cold 🏦

Wells Fargo's updated Online Access Agreement, effective 24 November, says customers are "solely responsible" for "actions resulting from incomplete, inaccurate, or manipulated inputs."
"Manipulated inputs" is prompt injection. A web page or email hides an instruction, the AI assistant reads it, and it acts. Under these terms, the bank has written the cost of that attack onto the customer.


The interesting part is Citi. Its Online User Agreement now has a Section H on third-party AI agents. If you give an agent your login and those credentials are "shared, leaked, or otherwise distributed", Citi "will consider any access and actions taken with the Online Credentials as authorized by You."

In plain words: if your AI provider is breached, the attacker's transfers count as yours.

But here's where it gets sharper:

- Citi has no obligation to investigate those actions "even if" they "conflict with any prompts or other instructions" you gave the agent 
- Citi's own AI tools are explicitly exempt from these terms 
- Wells Fargo says it does "not monitor, screen, or review AI Agent activities" 
- To revoke an agent, Wells Fargo says you "must retain evidence of such revocation"

TechCrunch reports PNC changed its terms on 18 November and Citizens emailed customers, after JPMorgan and Bank of America moved in October.

To be fair to the banks, credential sharing is a real risk, and both texts carve out "applicable law", so protections like Regulation E may still apply. No court has tested this yet that I could find.

And here's what concerns me. The industry spent a year debating whether models can resist prompt injection. The banks have quietly answered a different question: who pays when they cannot.

The lesson for anyone building or using agents: the security boundary can't sit inside the model. It has to sit in what the agent is allowed to touch.

- Never hand an agent your password - Prefer read-only or scoped API access - Treat revocation as a security control, with proof

The agent isn't the risk. The password you gave it is.

None of these were confirmed cyberattacks. Microsoft says its outage was not linked to any cyberattack. The investigations are still ongoing, so we'll see.

My take: we spend so much time planning for attackers that we forget to plan for plain failure.

But look at the result... When one system fails, everything connected to it feels it.
Cybersecurity isn't only about stopping attackers. It's also about staying up when something breaks.

text:
Hello everyone-It’s been a minute since my last post and these last few months have been some of the most exciting, interesting, difficult and enlightening. I had no idea on how badly I needed a reboot after spending 30-years at the same company. I’m still deciding my next chapter but have a few things on which I am working. As many of you know, I have been passionate about digital assets for many years. Regulation largely kept banks from participating in the space, but with the GENIUS Act, all of that has changed and banks are playing catch up. Between the convergence of AI, blockchain and deregulation—I believe the whole banking industry will be in a race for survival. Below are some of my thoughts on where all of this is heading.

The Banking Industry’s Biggest Advantage is about to Disappear.

For a century, banks have had a valid business model based mainly on one core feature: cheap deposits. Customers leave billions in checking and savings earning little or nothing, because moving money is a hassle and nobody watches it every day.

AI agents (bots) and blockchain end that or at very least create a major hurdle to that inertia from which banks benefit.

An AI agent can read your transaction history and your inbox. It sees the invoice that’s due Friday, the payroll on the 15th, the tax payment next month. It keeps every dollar in the highest-yielding place available. Then, on stablecoin rails that settle in seconds, 24/7, it moves to your checking account exactly when it’s needed and not a day sooner.

In fact, I envision a day when interest will be earned not by each day or quarter, but by the minute or even second. Why would anyone keep money in a checking account if funds could be held in a tokenized money market fund earning interest by the minute at the rate of SOFR and that same token can be used to buy a cheeseburger for lunch.

Idle balances become a thing of the past.

Some banks are blocking it. JPMorgan Chase, Citi, Bank of America and Charles Schwab have all said outside AI agents can’t move customer money. Schwab reports blocking Meta’s agent dozens of times a week.

Others are embracing it.
Robinhood: agent-only trading accounts and an agentic credit card
Mercury: agents can send transfers and payments through ChatGPT and Claude
Meow: agents can send ACH, wires and international payouts
@Ramp: Agent Cards and Agent Keys
Coinbase: Agentic Wallets and the x402 payments protocol
Stripe: an agent wallet in Link

Blocking buys time. It doesn’t stop customers from leaving for the institutions that say yes.

Soon I’ll post on what my best guess on the potential impact to the industry if banks were forced to pay market rates for funding. Ultimately, banks can win; however, it will require a new way of thinking and a desire to lean in and level up to new technologies and processes.

Que venza una deuda no es noticia. Lo que cambia esta vez es la tasa a la que se renueva:

• Buena parte de esos créditos se firmó en 2021 y 2022, a tasas cercanas al 4%.

Durante tres años los bancos prefirieron estirar plazos. Esa paciencia se está acabando, y muchas de esas negociaciones van a terminar en una venta.

No todo lo que se vende con apuro es una oportunidad. En oficinas, hoteles y edificios de departamentos con deuda a tasa variable, el activo mismo perdió valor. Ahí hay que ir con mucho cuidado.

Lo que me interesa está en otro lugar: el local comercial arrendado a una sola empresa, con contrato de más de 10 años. Quien compró en 2021 un activo que rentaba 5% y lo financió al 3,5% ganaba con cada dólar prestado. Si hoy tiene que refinanciar al 7%, le toca poner más equity o vender.

El arrendatario sigue pagando puntualmente. El contrato sigue siendo bueno. Lo que se acabó fue el apalancamiento a favor. Ese es el vendedor que va a aparecer en 2027: no vende por el inquilino, vende por la tasa, y va a aceptar un precio que hace dos años habría rechazado.

Three outages. One week.

Thursday, Microsoft went down for hours, and the cause was an upgrade gone wrong.
Friday, the FAA grounded every departing flight in the country for four and a half hours. Nearly 3,500 flights sat on the ground, and officials pointed straight at aging technology that got overloaded.
Today, customers at Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and others couldn’t get into their accounts. JPMorgan blamed a software bug.

This isn’t a doomsday post. Planes landed safely. Money didn’t vanish. But it’s worth paying attention.

Air traffic control is the clearest example. The problem was obvious for years, and it didn’t feel urgent until it was. Now there’s $12.5 billion on the table, with calls for more, to fix something that was cheaper to ignore than to replace.

Every business has its own version of that: the system nobody wants to touch because it still works. Thursday showed the other side too. Modernizing carries risk, and rushing it can break things. Putting it off just makes the bill bigger.

The goal isn’t flashy tech. It’s foundations you actually understand, upgrades you plan for instead of reacting to, and a clear answer to one question:

What’s the system your business can’t lose for a day, and when did someone last look at it closely?

text:
Four of the biggest US financial institutions shut outside AI agents out of customer accounts in a single week: JPMorganChase, Bank of Americaa, Citi and Charles Schwab.
It's easy to read this as banks vs. AI. It isn’t.

Look at what they actually blocked: agents logging in with the customer’s own username and password. That’s screen scraping with a smarter client. The bank can’t tell the agent from the customer, can’t limit what it does, and can’t revoke it without resetting the customer’s credentials.
JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon put it plainly on the earnings call: “you don’t want rogue agents and there could be thousands of them.”
Now look at what they left open. Read-only access through Plaid and open banking connectors is still allowed. Schwab CEO Rick Wurster says they’re building MCP servers so a client’s model can check balances under Schwab’s rules. Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan wants a human approving any money that leaves an account.
Put those together, and you have the outline of a standard:
- The agent gets its own identity, separate from the customer’s, and it’s temporary: issued for the task and gone when the task is done
- Access is delegated and scoped: read balances yes, move money no
- Anything that moves money triggers an out-of-band approval from the customer. CIBA already does this.
- Every token says which agent is acting and on whose behalf, so liability has somewhere to land
Yes, $1.6T in non-interest-bearing deposits is probably part of the motivation too. But the authorization gap is real, and it’s the part we already have standards for.
The liability question Bank of America is working through gets a lot simpler when the token carries the answer.
Source: PYMNTS, citing the Financial Times and Bloomberg [link in comments]
